Opposition, Invalidation or Purchase? A Cost-and-Time Decision Table for Squatted Marks

Discovering that someone else has filed or registered your mark in China is not one problem with one answer. Opposition, invalidation, non-use cancellation, a negotiated purchase and a fresh application differ in timing, control, evidence and risk.

Five Routes, One Decision

Discovering that someone else has filed or registered your mark in China is not a single problem with a single answer. There are five realistic routes, and they differ less in cost than in timing, control, evidence and risk: opposition against a published application, invalidation against a registration, non-use cancellation, a negotiated purchase or assignment, and a fresh application, sometimes with a renamed mark.

The right choice depends on where the conflicting right sits. A mark that is only at the publication stage is a different problem from one that has been registered for years and never used, and both differ from a registration held by a former distributor who is willing to sell. Start by establishing the status of the conflicting mark, your own prior rights, and the commercial deadline you are actually working to.

Two Article references frame the analysis. Article 20 refuses a mark identical or similar to an earlier registered or applied-for mark, and Article 24 protects prior legitimate rights and addresses bad-faith squatting. In practice, the strength of your evidence about prior use and reputation in China decides which routes are even available.

The Decision Table

The table below is deliberately qualitative. It compares the routes on four axes that you can assess before instructing counsel; it does not quote fees, success rates or how long proceedings take, because those depend on the case, the official fee schedules in force and the current rules. Confirm any figure against the official announcements and rules at the time you act.

RouteTimingControlEvidence burdenPrincipal risk
OppositionEarliest, fixed short statutory window from publicationHigh; you set the grounds and timingModerate; prior rights and reputationMissing the window; no second chance on the same application
InvalidationLater; subject to a statutory limitation period with an exception for bad-faith filings of well-known marksHigh; full grounds can be arguedHigh; reputation, bad faith and prior rightsEvidence-heavy; outcome uncertain
Non-use cancellationAvailable once the registration has been unused for the statutory period; the authority may also act on its own initiativeMedium; a third party or the authority may drive itShifts to the registrant to prove genuine useDoes not by itself give you a registration
Purchase or assignmentNegotiated; no fixed statutory timetableHighest; commercial terms are yours to setLow, but the transfer is examinedApproval may be refused; price and leverage
Fresh application or renameImmediate, but starts a new filingMedium; depends on clearing a new markLow for the filing; higher if arguing acquired distinctivenessAbandoning the original name; residual conflict remains

Use the table to shortlist, not to decide. Most real cases combine routes: an opposition plus a protective new filing, or a cancellation alongside a negotiated purchase. The combinations are where control and risk are actually managed.

When Opposition Fits

Opposition is the route with the shortest fuse and the best leverage: you challenge the application before it matures into a registration. Under the revised law the opposition period is reduced from three months to two months from preliminary publication with effect from 1 January 2027. That is the whole detection-to-filing chain, not a warning period.

It therefore only works if the watch, the decision authority and the evidence pack already exist. A brand that reviews the register occasionally will lose the window before its first internal meeting. Pre-authorise local counsel, log publication dates, and keep prior-rights and reputation documents ready so that only the conflicting application needs to be added.

The trade-off is that the grounds are argued on a relatively thin factual record and the other side can still respond. Where the conflict is clear and the evidence is strong, that is a good exchange. For the operating procedure see the 2-month opposition watch SOP.

When Invalidation or Cancellation Fit

Once the mark is registered, invalidation and non-use cancellation do the heavy lifting. Article 51 sets a five-year limitation period for requesting invalidation, but a bad-faith registration of a well-known mark is not subject to that five-year limit. That distinction often decides whether the route is open at all, so establish the registration date and the basis of the challenge first.

Article 57 addresses cancellation where a registered mark has become the generic name of the goods or has not been used for three consecutive years without justified reason, and it allows the authority to cancel on its own initiative. A cancellation is attractive against a blocker that never traded, but it clears an obstacle rather than granting you a right, so plan the filing that follows.

Both routes are evidence-heavy. Invalidation turns on prior rights, reputation in China and the applicant's bad faith; cancellation turns on whether genuine use exists on the designated goods. Keep dated, contract-backed records rather than assembling a file after the dispute starts. For what counts as valid use evidence see the non-use cancellation evidence guide.

When to Negotiate or Refile

A negotiated purchase is often the fastest route to certainty and the one where you keep the most control: you decide the price, the scope of the assignment and any coexistence or transition terms. It is not, however, a purely private transaction. Under Article 46, an assignment that is likely to cause confusion or have other adverse effects is not approved, so the transfer is examined rather than simply recorded. Journal the commercial logic, keep the assignment documents clean, and confirm the current filing formalities before relying on the transfer.

A fresh application, sometimes with a renamed mark, is the pragmatic choice where the original sign is weak, the evidence is thin, or the commercial timetable cannot wait for a dispute. It is immediate, but it concedes ground: you may lose the name consumers already know, and a residual conflicting right can still block or narrow the new filing. Clear the new candidate first, including its Chinese-character version.

Decide the sequence, not just the route. Opposition, invalidation, cancellation, purchase and refiling are frequently used together, and the order changes both control and exposure. We have deliberately kept this comparison qualitative: do not rely on quoted fees, success rates or processing times from third-party summaries, and ask your adviser for the position under the current official rules.

Sources and Caveats

Basis: Articles 20, 24, 36, 46, 51 and 57 of the Trademark Law of the PRC (2026 Revision) (adopted 26 June 2026, effective 1 January 2027); general practitioner guidance on responding to squatted marks. The two-month opposition period applies from 1 January 2027; the five-year invalidation limit, its well-known-mark exception, the three-year non-use rule and the Article 46 assignment test are statutory frameworks, not predictions of outcome. This article intentionally makes only a qualitative comparison of timing, control, evidence and risk: it quotes no fees, success rates or processing durations. Confirm the current official announcements and rules before acting. This is general information, not legal advice.
